accuracy.evidence: Figures are taken from Roediger and Karpicke (2006), Experiment 2: after 5 minutes SSSS 83%, SSST 78%, STTT 71%; after one week 40%, 56% and 61%, verified against the published paper. Working memory capacity of about four chunks follows Cowan (2001). The forgetting curve shape (steep, then levelling) follows Ebbinghaus (1885) and the Murre and Dros (2015) replication; the lab's curve is an exponential model and is labelled 'A simple model, not real data' on screen.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the beliefs the topic names and common study errors: that re-reading and highlighting are the best ways to study because the page feels familiar, that cramming the night before works, that forgetting means you are bad at a subject, that long-term memory gets full, that random digits are easy because they are small, and that a lesson once forgotten is gone. Each has its own corrective feedback in the challenge.

lab_distinct.evidence: Mechanics specific to memory: a four-slot desk that pushes old items off as new ones arrive, cutting FBIBBCUSA where slot cost depends on whether long-term memory knows the chunk, placing up to three reviews on a live forgetting-curve graph against a 40% line, revealing real study bars at two delays, and linking a new word to meaningful versus random cues. The distinctness gate passed against all existing labs, including Teaching It Back and Checking Your Own Work.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each principle is discovered by doing: the desk visibly drops '7' and 'dog' when overloaded; uncut letters need 9 slots but known chunks need 3; reviews placed on days 5 and 6 fail because the curve crosses the line on day 1.4, while day 1 then day 3 keeps it above all week, showing early then widening gaps; the 5-minute bars favour re-reading but the 1-week bars reverse. Every completed step states the rule in one sentence.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong answers: whether working memory holds about 4 or about 20 things, whether most of a lesson is left after one day without review, and whether reading four times or reading once and recalling three times wins a week later. The reveal quotes the learner's pick and the evidence that settles it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions (12-digit code, when forgetting is fastest, why re-reading feels useful, a test-week plan, chunking 1945, forgetting half a lesson) with a specific reason for every wrong option, for example 'Re-reading felt best but lost after a week: 40% against 61% for recall.' and 'Long-term memory is huge. The limit is the small desk of working memory.'

readability.evidence: Learner explanation uses short sentences and concrete images (a desk, a store, a path back) and passed the content gate's readability check for the 11-12 learner band; the adult text is plain and names each mistake. Lab cards are one or two sentences, and percentages are shown with labels rather than in text.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate reported no filler. Each kid paragraph covers one evidence statement: working versus long-term memory, chunking from prior knowledge, the forgetting curve with spaced review, and why re-reading feels useful but often is not. The adult text names five concrete mistakes and a recall-at-home routine.

mobile.evidence: Headless walkthrough completed all six steps and the challenge without page errors. Android 360px light and dark and iPhone 13 screenshots were checked mid-step; the link step first had cue cards overlapping the centre word and lines drawn over text, so it was relaid as a two-column grid with opaque cards. Every canvas target has a full-width button twin below.

accessibility.evidence: axe found no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. The canvas aria-label and live status line report state such as 'Slots needed 3 of 4', 'Reviews on day 1, 3. Lowest point 53 percent. Above the line all week.' and the revealed percentages, every tap has a labelled button alternative, and reduced motion shortens demo timing.
